newsitem.title: USA: Lawmaker urges N.J. drop Credit Suisse.
newsitem.headline: Lawmaker urges N.J. drop Credit Suisse.

text.p: A New Jersey lawmaker has urged Gov. Christine Whitman to drop Credit Suisse First Boston from a proposed financial transaction, citing accusations the firm's parent "plundered Holocaust victims' money during World War Two."
"Credit Suisse is at the core of this historical travesty," Neil Cohen, the New Jersey Assembly's Deputy Minority Leader, said in calling for the bank's ouster.
Credit Suisse First Boston is a unit of Credit Suisse Group.

New Jersey selected First Boston as an adviser on the deal, a proposed sale of the state's Temporary Disability Insurance program. The sale is designed to generate about $200 million of budget savings for the fiscal 1998 budget.
The plan itself has received little support in the state Legislature, and Cohen opposed it even before raising the Holocaust issue.
But Cohen, a Democrat from Elizabeth, said he wrote Whitman urging her to replace First Boston if the deal goes through.

"We must stand up to the powerful Swiss banking industry and send a clear message that the injustice they are imposing on Holocaust survivors will not be tolerated," Cohen said. "By hiring Credit Suisse of Boston to represent this state in the TDI sale, this administration is turning its back on its Jewish constituency."

Dave Kehler, New Jersey's associate deputy treasurer, said the state has no plans to drop First Boston from the deal. Kehler said Credit Suisse has taken steps to address the accusations, and has earned praise from Jewish organizations for its efforts to provide relief to survivors of the Holocaust.

Bob O'Brien, a managing director at Credit Suisse, said, "We are very sensitive to the underlying issues relative to all of these concerns, and we believe that our record demonstrates that we have acted in a very responsible way.
"We believe that it has been received that way by the relevent regulatory, legislative and Jewish community organizations," O'Brien said in an interview.

Allegations such as Cohen's have rocked Swiss banks in recent months, as government officials and Holocaust survivors said banks hoarded unclaimed wealth from Holocaust victims and secretly profited from the war.

In response, the Swiss government in February approved a Holocaust memorial fund, which plans to distribute millions of dollars in humanitarian aid to victims of Nazism. The three biggest Swiss banks, including Credit Suisse, helped launch the fund with a 100 million Swiss franc donation.
Credit Suisse has also agreed to abide by the findings of the Volker Commission, which is investigating the allegations.
In March, Cohen co-sponsored legislation in New Jersey that would severely restrict the state's dealings with Swiss companies or firms doing business with them.
Sponsors of the bill said it would stay in committee with no votes taken, unless the Swiss banks fail to make good on their promises to cooperate with the compensation efforts.

But Cohen said the reasoning behind his decision not to move forward on that bill does not apply to the insurance fund sale. Cohen said the March bill was an attempt to put the state's existing dealings with the banks on hold while the issues played out.
But the sale of the insurance fund would be a new transaction not covered by that decision, Cohen said.

"Just in case anyone thinks that by virtue of holding (the March bill) that we were backing off of anything, this sends an additional message, that our views should not be dismissed and that everything should be placed on hold until there's some meaningful resolution."
